title: 3Sum
directAnswer: Return all unique triplets that sum to zero. The interview-grade answer is: sort the array, fix one number with an outer loop, then two-pointer the rest of the array for the remaining pair that sums to its negation. Skip duplicate values at every level to keep triplets unique. O(n²) time, O(1) extra space (ignoring the output and sort).

remember.pattern: Sort + fix one + two pointers, skip duplicates
remember.formula:
sort(nums)
for i in range(n):
    if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i-1]: continue   # skip dup anchor
    l, r = i+1, n-1
    while l < r:
        s = nums[i] + nums[l] + nums[r]
        if s < 0: l += 1
        elif s > 0: r -= 1
        else: record; skip dup l and r; l += 1; r -= 1
rules: **Sort first** — it's what enables two pointers and makes duplicate-skipping trivial.
Skip a duplicate **anchor** with `if i > 0 and nums[i] == nums[i-1]: continue`.
After recording a triplet, skip duplicate `l` and `r` values before moving both pointers.
Move `l` right when the sum is too small, `r` left when too big — sortedness makes this monotonic.
Break early once `nums[i] > 0`: with a sorted array, three non-negative numbers can't sum to zero.
whenToUse: Find triplets / k-tuples that hit a target sum
Array is unsorted but you're allowed to sort (indices don't matter — values do)
You need *all unique* combinations, not just one match
A nested-loop pair search inside a fixed element can be collapsed with two pointers
antiSignals: Need the original indices, not values → sorting destroys them; use a hash map (that's Two Sum)
Only one pair, not all triplets → Two Sum hash map is simpler
Array already sorted and you need a single pair → plain two pointers (Two Sum II)
remember.takeaway: 3Sum is Two Sum II wrapped in an outer loop: fix one number, then solve a sorted two-pointer Two Sum for its negative. The reusable moves are 'sort to unlock two pointers' and 'skip equal neighbours to dedupe' — they extend straight to 4Sum and 3Sum Closest.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you reduce a triple-sum to a fixed element plus a sorted two-pointer Two Sum, and whether you can dedupe triplets cleanly without a hash set on the output.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Producing duplicate triplets (e.g. forgetting to skip equal anchors or equal pointer values), or defaulting to a brute-force O(n³) triple loop.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the O(n³) brute force, then 'sorting lets me fix one and two-pointer the rest for O(n²)'. Explain each duplicate-skip and the early break when nums[i] > 0.

problemStatement:
Given an integer array `nums`, return all the triplets `[nums[i], nums[j], nums[k]]` such that `i != j`, `i != k`, and `j != k`, and `nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] == 0`.

Notice that the solution set must **not contain duplicate triplets**.
understanding: Find every distinct combination of three values (by value, not index) that adds to zero. The hard part isn't finding triplets — it's returning each unique triplet exactly once even when the array has repeated values.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I return indices or the actual values?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Values — the triplets themselves. That's why we're free to sort the array.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Should the output contain duplicate triplets?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. [-1, 0, 1] must appear once even if multiple index combinations produce it. Dedupe is the core challenge.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can the same element be reused within a triplet?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — the three positions must be distinct indices, though their values may coincide (e.g. [0, 0, 0]).

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the array sorted?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Assume not. I'll sort it myself; since we return values, not indices, sorting is free to do.

diagrams.title: Picking the right approach
diagrams.caption: Sorting unlocks the two-pointer collapse of the inner pair search. The hash-set-on-output idea works but wastes memory.

approaches.name: Brute Force — Triple Loop With a Dedupe Set
approaches.whenToMention: Say it first to establish the baseline and to motivate why sorting + two pointers is the upgrade.
hints: The most literal reading: try every combination of three distinct indices and keep the ones that sum to zero.
Three nested loops i < j < k. For each triple, test nums[i] + nums[j] + nums[k] == 0.
To avoid duplicate triplets, sort each found triplet and store it in a set before collecting — but notice that's a lot of wasted work.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Choosing 3 of n indices is C(n,3) ≈ n³/6 combinations. Sorting each triplet and hashing it into a set adds the O(n) space for the dedupe structure.
approaches.explanation:
Enumerate every triple of indices `i < j < k` and keep those whose values sum to zero. Because the same triplet of values can arise from different index combinations, normalize each hit (sort its three numbers) and store it in a set so duplicates collapse.

**Why this is the natural first attempt.** 'Three numbers that sum to zero' maps directly to three nested loops. It's obviously correct, and stating it shows you can establish a baseline before reaching for cleverness.

**Why the dedupe is awkward.** The brute force has no structure to exploit, so the only way to keep triplets unique is to canonicalize each one (sort it) and dump it into a hash set. That's extra time per triplet and O(n) extra memory — a smell that the algorithm is fighting the problem rather than using it.

**Why we don't ship this.** With `n = 3000`, n³/6 is about 4.5 billion iterations — far too slow. The cubic factor and the bolt-on dedupe are exactly what sorting eliminates: once sorted, duplicates sit next to each other and the inner pair search collapses to two pointers.
approaches.insight: The brute force needs a set purely to fight duplicates. That pain is the signal: if the data were sorted, equal values would be adjacent and dedupe would be a cheap neighbour comparison — which is the whole reason the optimal sorts first.

approaches.name: Sort + Two Pointers (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want. Phrase it as 'sort, fix the first number, then run a sorted two-pointer Two Sum for the rest'.
hints: If the array were sorted, finding a pair that sums to a target is O(n) with two pointers (Two Sum II). How can you reuse that for a triple?
Sort the array. Fix the first element nums[i]; now you need two more numbers summing to -nums[i] in the suffix — exactly sorted Two Sum.
Walk l from i+1 and r from the end: move l up if the sum is too small, r down if too big. After a hit, skip equal neighbours on both pointers (and skip equal anchors) to avoid duplicate triplets.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Sorting is O(n log n). The outer loop runs n times and each inner two-pointer scan is O(n), giving O(n²) which dominates. Aside from the output and the in-place sort, only a few indices are stored → O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Sort the array first. Then iterate an anchor index `i` from left to right. For each anchor, the remaining problem is 'find two numbers in the suffix `i+1 .. n-1` that sum to `-nums[i]`' — and because the suffix is sorted, that's a classic two-pointer scan with `l = i+1` and `r = n-1`.

**Why sorting is the unlock.** Two Sum on an *unsorted* array needs a hash map. But on a *sorted* array, two pointers solve it in O(1) space: if the current sum is too small, the only way to grow it is to move the left pointer right (to a larger value); if it's too big, move the right pointer left. Sortedness makes the search monotonic, so each pointer sweeps the suffix once. Wrapping that in the outer anchor loop turns an O(n³) problem into O(n²).

**How duplicates are killed, level by level.** Sorting places equal values next to each other, so dedupe becomes neighbour comparison instead of a hash set:
- *Anchor dedupe*: if `nums[i] == nums[i-1]`, this anchor would reproduce every triplet the previous anchor already found — skip it.
- *Pointer dedupe*: after recording a triplet, advance `l` past any values equal to the one just used, and pull `r` back past any equal values, so the same pair isn't recorded twice.

**Why the early break helps.** Once `nums[i] > 0`, the anchor and everything to its right are positive (array is sorted), so no triplet starting here can sum to zero. Breaking out skips a chunk of useless work.

**Why O(1) extra space.** We sort in place and use only the indices `i`, `l`, `r`. The returned list isn't counted as auxiliary space, and unlike the brute force we need no dedupe set.
approaches.insight: 3Sum = an outer loop over Two Sum II. The two reusable moves — 'sort to convert a hash-map pair search into an O(1)-space two-pointer scan' and 'skip equal neighbours to dedupe' — generalize directly: add another outer loop and the same machinery solves 4Sum in O(n³).

pitfalls: Forgetting any of the three duplicate skips → duplicate triplets in the output.
Skipping the anchor with `i >= 0` instead of `i > 0` — skips the very first element wrongly.
Comparing nums[l] to nums[l+1] (not yet visited) instead of nums[l-1] when deduping after the move.

commonMistakes: Emitting duplicate triplets by not skipping equal anchors and equal pointer values.
Defaulting to the O(n³) triple loop on an input where n can be 3000.
Sorting but then comparing the wrong neighbour when deduping the pointers.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Not skipping the duplicate anchor
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If two equal anchors are processed, every triplet found for the first is regenerated for the second, producing duplicates.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Not deduping the pointers after a hit
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When the suffix has repeated values, the same (l, r) value pair can be recorded multiple times unless you skip equal neighbours.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting to sort before two pointers
commonMistakesDetailed.why: The two-pointer convergence relies on monotonic sums; on an unsorted array, moving l or r doesn't reliably grow or shrink the sum.
